subsection: 3. The Irish in the USA and Britain: anti-Irish sentiment and political participation

notes.b: Hostility to the Irish rested on religion, poverty and competition for work, and it was reinforced by stereotypes that were widely printed.
points: Religion: most Irish emigrants were Catholic, and Protestant Americans and Britons often saw Catholicism as foreign and a threat to their institutions.
Poverty and disease: the Irish who arrived in the Famine years were poor, and outbreaks of cholera and typhus were blamed on them.
Crime and drink: Irish migrants were blamed for crime, drunkenness and disorder in the cities where they lived.
Competition for work: Irish labourers and servants competed with native-born and other workers, and this created resentment among them.
Racial stereotypes: the Irish were portrayed as racially inferior, and in cartoons they were often drawn with apelike features.

notes.h: Anti-Irish sentiment in the United States
notes.b: American nativism, the movement against immigrants and Catholic influence, reached its height in the 1840s and 1850s and continued in cartoons and job notices afterwards.
points: The Philadelphia riots of 1844 were anti-Catholic disturbances in which Irish Catholic churches and homes were attacked by nativist mobs.
Nativism grew into a political movement, and the Know-Nothings, formally the American Party, won major state victories in 1854, including Massachusetts.
The Know-Nothings took their name from the secrecy of their members, who were told to say they knew nothing when questioned about the movement.
Job advertisements and signs in the 19th century often stated “No Irish Need Apply”, excluding Irish applicants from work.
Thomas Nast’s cartoons in Harper’s Weekly in the 1870s and 1880s portrayed Irish Catholics, and especially Irish politicians, as ape-like and corrupt.

notes.b: In Britain anti-Irish feeling was mixed with sectarian rivalry, and it flared at moments of Fenian threat.
points: Punch magazine caricatured the Irish in the 1840s and 1860s, presenting them as simian, violent and backward.
The Stockport riots of 1852 saw Irish Catholics attacked in Stockport, with houses and property damaged in anti-Irish violence.
In Liverpool and Glasgow, Protestant Orange lodges and Catholic Irish communities clashed, and sectarian rivalry shaped local politics and street life.
After the Fenian rising of 1867, the Clerkenwell explosion in London that December led to fears that all Irish people in Britain were a security threat.
Fenian scares led to heavy policing of Irish districts, and Irish nationalists claimed that the state treated the whole community as suspect.

notes.h: Irish political participation in the United States
notes.b: Irish Americans turned their numbers into political power through the Democratic Party and the city machines.
points: Most Irish Americans voted Democratic, because the party defended immigrants against nativist attacks and offered jobs and help.
Ward politics: local party organisers in each ward gave immigrants jobs, housing and legal help in return for votes.
Tammany Hall, the Democratic organisation in New York City, controlled city politics through patronage, jobs and contracts.
By the late 19th century Irish-American politicians had been elected mayors of cities including New York and Boston, and they sat in Congress.
Irish men were prominent in urban police forces and fire companies, and these jobs were a route into local politics.
Irish-American political success was built on group loyalty, and it gave immigrant communities a voice in city government.

notes.b: Richard Croker turned Tammany Hall into the most powerful political machine in New York City.
points: Richard Croker was born in County Cork in 1843 and was taken to New York as a child, where he grew up in a poor Irish district.
He rose through the fire companies and the local Democratic clubs, and he became the leader of Tammany Hall in the mid-1880s.
He ran Tammany Hall until 1901, using patronage, jobs in city departments and contracts to build support among immigrants and the poor.
As a participant in city politics, he controlled Democratic nominations and placed his allies in office, and his power depended on the police and the courts.
Contemporary reformers and much of the respectable press condemned Croker’s corruption, while many Tammany voters regarded him as a friend of the poor.
He retired to Ireland in later life, and historians now present him as the clearest example of machine politics, in which Irish-American political success came with corruption.
Historians also see his career as a route of upward mobility for an immigrant, although the cost to honest government was high.

notes.b: Joseph P. Kennedy showed how an Irish-American could rise to the top of business and then government, and his career was marked by controversy.
points: Joseph P. Kennedy was born in Boston in 1888, the son of Patrick J. Kennedy, a Boston politician and businessman.
He built a fortune in banking, shipbuilding and the film industry before entering government.
He was the first chairman of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, from 1934, to regulate the stock market after the crash of 1929.
In 1937 he led the US Maritime Commission, and in 1938 President Roosevelt appointed him ambassador to Britain.
As ambassador from 1938 to 1940 he took a pessimistic view of Britain’s chances in a war with Germany, and in November 1940 he resigned after remarks that Britain would not survive.
Contemporary Irish-American opinion was divided: some saw him as a success, while others distrusted him for his conservative views and his closeness to the British government.

Historians judge him a pragmatic appeaser whose pessimism shaped American thinking on Britain, and his sons, including John F. Kennedy, were shaped by his ambitions (see the notes on John F. Kennedy).

notes.b: Paul O’Dwyer combined a career as a New York lawyer with campaigns for civil rights and for Irish causes.
points: Paul O’Dwyer was a New York lawyer and Democratic politician, and he was the brother of William O’Dwyer, who was mayor of New York from 1946 to 1950.
He practised law in New York and took on civil rights cases and causes for working people and immigrants.
He was president of the New York City Council in the 1970s, a position he held after a long career in Democratic politics.
He was active in Irish causes, and in the 1970s and 1980s he criticised British policy in Northern Ireland.
Contemporaries saw him as a liberal and a critic of the establishment, and some criticised his views on Northern Ireland as too sympathetic to the republican cause.
Historians place him in the tradition of liberal Irish-American politics, in which civil rights and Irish nationalism were linked.

notes.b: The Irish vote in British cities was strongest in Liverpool and Scotland, and it was used by nationalist and Labour politicians.
points: T. P. O’Connor was elected MP for Liverpool Scotland in 1885, and he held the seat until 1929 as a nationalist and a journalist.
O’Connor founded newspapers in London, including The Star, and he used the press to support Home Rule and Irish causes.
Irish voters in Liverpool and Glasgow were largely Catholic and often supported the Irish Parliamentary Party or the Liberal Party.
From the early 20th century Irish voters in Britain increasingly backed the Labour Party, which also drew support from the working class.
The Irish in Britain were not treated as aliens, which meant they could vote and stand for Parliament as British subjects.

notes.b: The Molly Maguires were a secret society among Irish miners in the Pennsylvania anthracite coalfields, whose conflict with mine owners ended in executions.
points: The society operated in the anthracite coalfields of eastern Pennsylvania, especially in Schuylkill County, in the 1860s and 1870s.
Members used intimidation and violence against mine owners, mine bosses and those seen as informers, to press for better pay and conditions.
The Pinkerton detective James McParland infiltrated the society and gave evidence against its members at the trials.
The trials took place in Pennsylvania between 1875 and 1877, and convictions depended heavily on the evidence of informers.
About twenty men were hanged for murder, ten of them on a single day in June 1877.
Historians debate whether the Molly Maguires were a labour organisation, an Irish nationalist society or a criminal conspiracy, and the trials are read differently for each view.

notes.b: Judgements on Irish political life in America and Britain turn on whether the Irish gained real influence despite discrimination, or only built machines and patronage.
points: Achievement: Irish politicians built lasting power in American cities and in some British seats, and they gave immigrants a route into public life.
Limit: machine politics relied on patronage and corruption, and reform movements challenged it from the 1880s onwards.
Success against discrimination: by the early 20th century Irish Americans were prominent in the police and city government, a sign that discrimination was being overcome.
Contemporary view: nativists and reformers condemned Irish politicians as corrupt, while Irish communities defended them as champions of immigrants.
Later view: historians disagree on whether Irish political success advanced assimilation or delayed it, because machine politics kept communities separate.
